title: Sakya Pandita
hook: the scholar of the Sakya school, famous for his book of wise sayings

segments.voice: Yesterday, Yeshe Tsogyal, keeper of the hidden teachings. Your line was the great mother. Did you get to thank a woman who taught you something? Day nine hundred seventy-nine.

Some families have a few lines that get passed down. Measure twice, cut once. Don't go to bed angry. A grandmother said them so often that they stuck, and years later they come out of a grandchild's mouth at the oddest moments. Tibet has a book of lines like that, short verses of good sense, small enough to learn by heart. The man who wrote it was a celebrated scholar, a master of logic and debate. And he chose to put a lot of what he knew into sayings small enough to carry. Today, Sakya Pandita.
screen: `LINES THAT GET PASSED DOWN.` → `A TIBETAN BOOK OF GOOD SENSE.` → `A SCHOLAR WHO WROTE SMALL.`

segments.voice: First, the name. Sakya is a school of Tibetan Buddhism, named for the monastery at its center. Pandita is a Sanskrit title for a learned scholar. Tradition says Tibetans gave him that title because he mastered the Indian sciences, from grammar to logic. He also wrote a work on logic, the Treasury of Valid Reasoning. Second, the surprise. This same scholar wrote the Treasury of Good Sayings, a collection of short verses about everyday life: how the wise and the foolish behave, how to treat friends, how to hold wealth, how to speak. The verses lean on everyday pictures, from the house, the field and the road. Third, why a scholar would write this way. A long argument helps a student in the debating courtyard. A short saying goes home with the farmer and the trader, and comes back to mind when it's needed. One saying credited to him runs roughly like this: even if you will die tomorrow, study today; you may not become wise in this life, but it is like saving wealth for the next. Fourth, his life outside the library. Tradition says that late in life he traveled to the court of a Mongol prince, and that his teaching there helped shape how Mongol rulers and Tibetan teachers dealt with each other afterward. The man who wrote about speaking well, the story goes, was asked to practice it in a foreign court, far from home.
screen: `A SCHOOL, AND A TITLE FOR A SCHOLAR.` · `A TREASURY OF GOOD SAYINGS.` · `A SAYING GOES HOME WITH YOU.` · `WORDS CARRIED TO A MONGOL COURT.` · then, large: `WISDOM SMALL ENOUGH TO CARRY.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: learn one proverb. Settle, and breathe. Choose one short saying. It can be the one you just heard, about studying today even if you die tomorrow. Or one from your own family, your own grandmother, your own tradition. Say it once, quietly, or just in your head. Then say it again on the out-breath, slowly, letting each word land. Notice which word feels heaviest. Stay with that word for a few breaths. When your mind wanders, come back to the saying. The bell holds the time.
Sakya Pandita. The great scholar of the Sakya school, master of logic, who wrote the Treasury of Good Sayings so wisdom could travel in small pieces. Today's word.
Your line: wise sayings. Today, pass one good saying on to someone, and tell them where you got it. Day nine hundred seventy-nine.

howItsDone: In Tibetan communities, verses from Sakya Pandita's Treasury of Good Sayings are learned and quoted, and his work on logic is studied in monastic settings, especially in the Sakya school.

original.note: Sanskrit pandita: a learned one, a scholar. Tibetans gave him this title.

what it means: a great Sakya scholar who put teaching into short verses so anyone could carry it home.
what a scholar hears: the Treasury of Good Sayings stands beside his Treasury of Valid Reasoning; the same author wrote for the debate courtyard and for the household.
